newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Russia could lose military bases -Georgian speaker.
newsitem.headline: Russia could lose military bases -Georgian speaker.

text.p: Georgia's parliamentary speaker warned Russia on Monday that it would lose its military bases in the former Soviet republic if it gave new support to Abkhaz separatists.
Zurab Zhvaniya told reporters that Georgia did, however, want Russia to continue as a mediator in the unresolved conflict with the Abkhaz rebels even if its peacekeepers leave the region.
"We would like Russia to continue its mediating role," said Zhvaniya, seen as the second most powerful politician in the Transcaucasus state after President Eduard Shevardnadze.

"But a return to the policies of provocation and support for the separatists will mean a sharp worsening in Russo-Georgian relations, and it would be difficult to imagine a continuation of the presence of the Russian bases," he said.
Russia was allowed to keep three former Soviet bases in Georgia in exchange for a tacit promise to help Tbilisi regain control over Abkhazia, which it lost after a bitter 1992-93 war.
Georgian military officials say the bases contain at least 20,000 troops.

Russian officials decline to comment on the bases, which are strategically important for Moscow and completely separate from 1,500 Russian peacekeepers patrolling a buffer zone between Georgia and Abkhazia.
Georgia says the peacekeepers must start leaving after July 31 if they do not agree to do more, including helping Georgian refugees return home and patrolling more of Abkhazia.
A possible departure of the peacekeepers and the vacuum that might leave has left observers fearing new hostilities between the two sides.
Alleged Russian help for the Abkhaz during the conflict has been the source of much bad blood between Moscow and Tbilisi since Georgia gained independence.

Shevardnadze accused Russia of giving the separatists military help and equipment in order to help dismember his state and force it to join the Moscow-led Commonwealth of Independent States, which groups most former Soviet republics.
Russia denies the charges but some of its military officers still in the region have said they acted as advisers to the Abkhaz and provided them with weaponry.
Georgia and Abkhazia recently completed two weeks of intense negotiations in Moscow but failed to come up with a comprehensive plan to end their conflict.

Georgia says Abkhaz desires for a "union state" of two equal partners would give the pro-independence Sukhumi government a basis to secede later. It is offering Abkhazia a federative pact with strong autonomy, something the rebels reject.
Shevardnadze said in a radio address on Monday that direct contacts with the Abkhaz leadership and by way of Russian mediators was continuing.

Western diplomats say that the prospects are better now for resolving the conflict than at any time over the past three years, mostly because the two sides fear a re-ignition of the war which killed over 10,000 people in 1992-93.
"There is some very intense negotiating going on and I see more of a desire to get this issue resolved than ever," said one Western diplomat.
